slides.title: Urea
slides.eyebrow: Kidney function · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood

What it is used for: BUN is often part of a comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP) and helps diagnose or monitor kidney diseases. Because early kidney disease usually has no signs or symptoms, it is also used to screen people at risk.
BUN is often interpreted together with blood creatinine from the same panel (one of the test’s other names is BUN-to-creatinine ratio); this comparison can help find the cause of a kidney problem.

slides.title: Urea
slides.eyebrow: Kidney function · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: MedlinePlus covers this analyte as the BUN (blood urea nitrogen) test, which measures the amount of urea nitrogen in the blood. Urea nitrogen is a waste product formed as the body breaks down proteins; it is carried in blood and removed by the kidneys in urine.

slides.title: Urea
bullets: High: A high BUN generally suggests that the kidneys are not working well. Other possible causes include dehydration, burns, certain medicines, a high-protein diet and a recent heart attack.
Low: Possible causes of a low BUN include a lack of protein in the diet, malnutrition and liver disease.

slides.title: Urea
bullets: Pre-analytics: Usually no special preparation is needed. If other tests are ordered on the same blood sample, fasting for several hours may be required.
Limitations: BUN levels vary with sex and usually increase with age. An abnormal result does not always mean a condition that needs treatment.
BUN is only one measure of kidney function. If kidney disease is suspected, other tests may be needed, such as creatinine and GFR, which estimates how well the kidneys filter blood.

slides.title: Creatinine
slides.eyebrow: Kidney function · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Blood (serum) and/or urine  ·  Units: mg/dL, µmol/L

What it is used for: Used to check kidney health, help diagnose kidney disease, monitor known kidney problems and how treatment is working, and check for side effects of medicines that may affect the kidneys. Blood creatinine may be measured alone or within a basic (BMP) or comprehensive (CMP) metabolic panel.

eGFR calculated from blood creatinine reflects kidney health more accurately than creatinine alone. Creatinine clearance (comparing blood and urine creatinine) is less accurate than eGFR but may help in people with very high muscle mass or loss of muscle mass (age, illness, limb loss).

slides.title: Creatinine
slides.eyebrow: Kidney function · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Urine creatinine is used to calculate the urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR). Comparing blood creatinine with BUN measured in the same panel can help find the cause of a kidney problem.

NIDDK suggests that laboratories report eGFR whenever serum creatinine is measured. To reduce rounding errors in eGFR equations, creatinine is rounded to two decimal places in mg/dL or to the nearest whole number in µmol/L.

Physiology: Creatinine is a normal waste product made when muscles are used and some muscle tissue breaks down. The kidneys filter it from blood into urine; if the kidneys are not working well, creatinine can build up in blood and less may appear in urine.

slides.title: Creatinine
bullets: High: Possible kidney-related causes of high blood creatinine: kidney disease or injury (including infection, poor blood flow to the kidneys, a blockage in the urinary system or kidney failure) and conditions that affect the kidneys, such as heart failure or diabetes.

High: High creatinine does not always mean a kidney problem: dehydration, muscle disorders and injuries, muscular dystrophy, intense exercise or a diet high in meat can raise it. Certain health problems in pregnancy can also increase creatinine.

slides.title: Creatinine
bullets: Low: Low blood creatinine is uncommon. Possible causes include malnutrition, conditions that make muscles smaller (a long illness, a nerve disorder, muscle loss from aging) and serious liver disease.

slides.title: Creatinine
bullets: Pre-analytics: The person may be asked not to eat meat for 24 hours before the test, because meat can temporarily raise creatinine. If creatinine is part of a BMP or CMP, fasting for up to 12 hours may be needed.
Urine creatinine may require collecting all urine over 24 hours, because creatinine levels vary through the day. During collection the container is kept in a refrigerator or a cooler with ice.
Interferences: Certain medicines and supplements can affect the result, so everything the person takes should be reported.

slides.title: Creatinine
bullets: Limitations: Creatinine alone is not the best way to assess kidney function, because creatinine production depends on muscle mass, diet, age and activity. Its results are therefore often used in calculations or compared with other substances.

A normal creatinine does not rule out kidney disease: it may stay in the normal range in early disease and rise as the disease becomes more serious. A single high result cannot diagnose a specific condition; retesting and/or other tests are usually needed.

slides.title: Uric acid
slides.eyebrow: Kidney function · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Blood or 24-hour urine

What it is used for: A blood test helps diagnose gout (usually together with synovial fluid analysis) and monitors uric acid during chemotherapy or other cancer treatment: when cancer cells are killed quickly they release large amounts of purines, and testing helps catch a rise early.
A urine test helps find out whether high uric acid is causing kidney stones and monitors the risk of kidney stones in people with gout.

slides.title: Uric acid
slides.eyebrow: Kidney function · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: Uric acid is a normal waste product formed when the body breaks down purines, which are released from dying cells and found in certain foods and drinks. Normally it dissolves in blood, is filtered by the kidneys and leaves the body in urine.

If the body makes too much uric acid or the kidneys remove too little, it builds up in blood and can form needle-shaped crystals in and around joints (gout). High levels can also cause kidney stones or kidney failure, but not everyone with high levels develops these problems.

slides.title: Uric acid
bullets: High: High blood uric acid may occur when the body makes too much or the kidneys cannot remove enough. Eating many purine-rich foods can also raise it: red and organ meats (liver, kidney), some seafood (shellfish, anchovies, sardines, trout, tuna), all types of alcohol and high-fructose corn syrup in soda and sweets.

High: Conditions that may be related to high blood uric acid include gout, kidney disease or kidney stones, leukemia, multiple myeloma, metastatic cancer, side effects of cancer treatment such as chemotherapy, alcohol use disorder and preeclampsia.

slides.title: Uric acid
bullets: High: High urine uric acid may be related to gout, kidney stones or a high risk of them, leukemia, multiple myeloma or metastatic cancer, obesity, or an inherited genetic condition such as Lesch–Nyhan syndrome.
Low: Low blood uric acid is uncommon and usually does not cause health problems; related conditions are usually diagnosed with other tests.
Low: Low urine uric acid may be related to kidney disease, lead poisoning or alcohol use disorder.

slides.title: Uric acid
bullets: Pre-analytics: The urine test requires collecting all urine for 24 hours: the first void is discarded and its time recorded, then all urine for the next 24 hours goes into the container. During collection the container is kept in a refrigerator or a cooler with ice.

Interferences: Many medicines, including aspirin, can affect uric acid levels in blood and urine, and taking niacin (vitamin B3) can also affect results. All medicines taken should therefore be reported.
Limitations: A high uric acid in blood or urine does not always mean a condition that needs treatment—many people have high levels without health problems. More tests may be needed to find the cause.

slides.title: Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR)
slides.eyebrow: Kidney function · What it is used for · 1/3
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (calculated value)  ·  Units: mL/min/1.73 m²

What it is used for: eGFR is used to screen for kidney disease in people without symptoms, help diagnose it in people with symptoms, find out how serious it is, monitor people treated for chronic kidney disease or taking medicines that could harm the kidneys, and check kidney health before treatments that could affect the kidneys.
NIDDK names eGFR and urine albumin as the two key markers of chronic kidney disease. The same two tests are used to monitor known kidney disease.

slides.title: Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR)
slides.eyebrow: Kidney function · What it is used for · 2/3
bullets: Physiology: The kidneys contain tiny filters (glomeruli) that remove waste and extra water from blood. eGFR usually starts from blood creatinine, but creatinine alone cannot determine eGFR because people make different amounts depending on size, diet and activity, so an equation combines it with personal data such as age and sex.

eGFR can also be calculated from cystatin C, a protein made by many cells whose level is not affected by muscle size, age or diet. NIDDK states that using both creatinine and cystatin C is preferred and more accurate than creatinine alone, especially when eGFR is near a critical decision value such as drug dosing or kidney transplant evaluation.

slides.title: Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR)
slides.eyebrow: Kidney function · What it is used for · 3/3
bullets: Measured GFR (mGFR) involves injecting a filtration marker and monitoring how quickly the kidneys clear it from blood. It is complicated and not widely available, so it is usually done only in special situations, such as extreme obesity or before donating a kidney.

slides.title: Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR)
slides.eyebrow: Kidney function · Reference values and decision limits
rows: People tested for kidney disease (NIDDK) — Less than 60 (60 or more is described as the normal range).
People tested for kidney disease (NIDDK) — 15 or less.

slides.title: Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR)
bullets: Low: If the kidneys filter waste too slowly (low eGFR), it may be a sign of damage from kidney disease. An eGFR lower than normal for the person may lead to further tests: urine protein, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, BUN, and kidney ultrasound or CT.

slides.title: Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR)
bullets: Pre-analytics: Preparation follows the provider’s instructions: fasting or avoiding certain foods such as meat for several hours may be required, because meat can affect the eGFR result. Certain medicines can also affect results, so all medicines should be reported.

Interferences: eGFR is not reliable with rapidly changing creatinine, extremes of muscle mass and body size, or altered diet patterns. MedlinePlus also lists severe malnutrition, muscle-wasting conditions, advanced liver disease and limb amputation; in such cases a measured GFR (mGFR) may be used.

slides.title: Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR)
bullets: Limitations: In some cases cystatin C is measured instead of creatinine: in people younger than 18 or over 65, with a lot of muscle mass, with obesity, or during pregnancy.
eGFR is an estimate, not a precise measure: it may not always reflect kidney damage, and an abnormal result can occur without damage. Trends in eGFR are therefore preferred over a single value.

NIDDK supports calculating eGFR with CKD-EPI equations that do not include a race coefficient. When values calculated with different equations are compared, part of the change may come from the equation rather than from kidney function.

slides.title: Chronic kidney disease (CKD)
bullets: Early kidney disease usually has no symptoms — only tests show how the kidneys work. Testing is needed with diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease or a family history of kidney failure; yearly with diabetes. Two key tests are used to diagnose and monitor: blood GFR and urine albumin.

slides.title: Chronic kidney disease (CKD)
rows: Estimates kidney filtration; calculated from creatinine.
Albumin passes into urine when the kidneys are damaged; UACR estimates daily albumin loss.
The basis for estimating GFR; it rises as kidney disease gets worse.

slides.title: Chronic kidney disease (CKD)
rows: Results are tracked over time: a stable GFR may mean treatment is working.
If urine albumin stays the same or goes down, treatment may be working.

slides.title: Chronic kidney disease (CKD)
rows: Kidney disease is possible; the clinician decides when to recheck.
Called kidney failure; most people at this level need dialysis or a kidney transplant.
May be a sign of kidney disease. If albumin is found, the test may be repeated once or twice to confirm.

slides.title: Chronic kidney disease (CKD)
bullets: Urine albumin can rise temporarily with exercise, certain medicines, fever and inflammation.

slides.title: Reference values and decision limits
rows: G1 ≥90; G2 60–89; G3a 45–59; G3b 30–44; G4 15–29; G5 <15 (if persisting >3 months) mL/min/1.73 m²

slides.title: Reference values and decision limits
rows: Analytical requirement for the creatinine method
CV <2.3%; bias <3.7%; calibration traceable to a reference material; enzymatic method preferred %

slides.title: A very muscular person who eats a lot of meat and trains intensely has blood creatinine above the laboratory interval. Which interpretation best fits the source?
options: Non-kidney factors (muscle, diet, intense exercise) may contribute; one result is not a diagnosis, so retesting or other tests such as eGFR are needed.
It points to serious liver disease.
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: the source says creatinine depends on muscle and diet, and intense exercise and a meat-rich diet can raise it.

Basis: MedlinePlus: high creatinine is not always a kidney problem (dehydration, muscle factors, intense exercise, meat-rich diet); a single high result is not a diagnosis.

slides.title: Why does a creatinine within the laboratory interval not rule out kidney disease?
options: In early kidney disease creatinine may stay in the normal range and rise only as the disease becomes more serious.
Creatinine is not removed by the kidneys.
Creatinine is meaningful only in urine, not in blood.
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: the source states exactly this; if kidney disease is suspected, other kidney tests are done.

Basis: MedlinePlus: blood creatinine may stay in the normal range in early kidney disease and rises as it becomes more serious.

slides.title: What does the BUN test actually measure?
options: Total protein in the blood, from which urea nitrogen is formed
Creatinine, a waste product released from muscle and removed by the kidneys
Urea nitrogen, a waste product of protein breakdown removed by the kidneys
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: BUN measures the amount of urea nitrogen in the blood.

Basis: MedlinePlus: the BUN test measures urea nitrogen in blood; urea nitrogen forms when proteins are broken down and is removed by the kidneys.

slides.title: A person who has been drinking very little fluid has a high BUN. Which statement matches the source?
options: A high BUN always means kidney disease, whatever the person’s fluid intake has been.
Dehydration is one possible cause of a high BUN, and an abnormal result does not always mean a condition needing treatment.
Dehydration typically lowers BUN rather than raising it, so this high result must reflect a kidney disease needing treatment.
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: dehydration is listed among causes of high BUN; if kidney disease is suspected, other tests may be needed.

Basis: MedlinePlus: dehydration is a possible cause of high BUN; abnormal results don’t always mean a condition needing treatment.

slides.title: Why is eGFR calculated with an equation rather than reading kidney function directly from blood creatinine?
options: People make different amounts of creatinine depending on size, diet and activity, so creatinine is combined with factors such as age and sex.
Creatinine is not filtered by the kidneys.
eGFR is measured directly after injecting a filtration marker.
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: per the source, creatinine alone cannot determine eGFR.

Basis: MedlinePlus: creatinine alone can’t determine eGFR because its production depends on size, diet and activity; mGFR uses an injected filtration marker.

slides.title: For a patient with a limb amputation or severe muscle wasting, what approach does the source describe?
options: Creatinine-based eGFR stays fully reliable, because muscle mass does not affect creatinine.
eGFR is dropped and BUN alone is used to judge kidney function.
eGFR may be unreliable; a measured GFR (mGFR) with a filtration marker may be used.
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: MedlinePlus lists limb amputation and muscle wasting among situations for mGFR.

Basis: MedlinePlus: in severe malnutrition, muscle wasting, advanced liver disease and amputation, eGFR may be unreliable and mGFR gives a clearer picture.

slides.title: Creatinine is:
options: the end product of protein metabolism

slides.title: When does residual nitrogen increase due to urea nitrogen:
options: nephritis, acute and chronic renal failure

Residual nitrogen. Azotemias. Clinical and diagnostic significance?
bullets: 1. "Residual nitrogen" is the nitrogen in the protein-free filtrate (urea ~50%, amino acids, uric acid, creatinine, ammonia, etc.); this summary parameter is historical, individual components are measured now.

2. Azotemia is an increase of nitrogenous substances (urea, creatinine) in the blood: prerenal (reduced renal perfusion – dehydration, heart failure, hemorrhage; the urea/creatinine ratio is usually >20:1 (in mg/dL)), renal (parenchymal damage), postrenal (urinary tract obstruction).
3. Productional (extrarenal) increase of urea: high protein intake, catabolism, GI bleeding, glucocorticoids.

slides.title: Residual nitrogen. Azotemias. Clinical and diagnostic significance?
bullets: 4. Assessing kidney function: creatinine (the enzymatic method is preferred) and eGFR, cystatin C if needed; urea and uric acid are auxiliary.
5. Decrease of urea: severe liver failure, protein deficiency, pregnancy, fluid overload.

slides.title: Methods of determining urea?
bullets: 1. The main method is enzymatic: urease cleaves urea into ammonia and CO2, and ammonia consumes NADH in the glutamate dehydrogenase reaction – the decrease in absorbance at 340 nm is measured kinetically.
2. Other variants: urease + conductometry or an ion-selective electrode; non-automated colorimetric methods (for example diacetyl monoxime) – historical.
3. Sample: serum/plasma (ammonium heparin is not used – ammonia contamination), urine.
4. Expressing the result: urea (mmol/L) or blood urea nitrogen (BUN, mg/dL); know the conversion.

slides.title: Methods of determining urea?
bullets: 5. Clinical significance: types of azotemia, urea/creatinine ratio (high in the prerenal state), dialysis adequacy; urea depends more on diet and catabolism than GFR does.

slides.title: Methods of determining creatinine?
bullets: 1. Jaffe method – the red-orange complex of creatinine with picrate in an alkaline medium; the kinetic variant reduces interference, but glucose, ketone bodies, bilirubin and some drugs ("non-creatinine chromogens") interfere.
2. Enzymatic methods (creatininase/creatinase/sarcosine oxidase–peroxidase) are more specific; KDIGO 2024 recommends the enzymatic method where possible (especially in children).
3. Standardization: calibration must be traceable to international reference materials (IDMS), CV <2.3%; separate plasma within 12 hours.

slides.title: Methods of determining creatinine?
bullets: 4. eGFR: calculated from creatinine (CKD-EPI 2021) and reported together with creatinine; <60 mL/min/1.73 m² is considered reduced; creatinine depends on muscle mass – eGFR together with cystatin C is more accurate.
5. Clinical significance: CKD and acute kidney injury; creatinine clearance and urine albumin/creatinine ratio.
